docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Last update: 20261008-1

This repository contains the material for a stripped-down and heavily personalized version of the O2 tutorial.

It is by no means meant to be a replacement for the centrally maintained O2 documentation, which can be found at this link.

docs.title: Access to CCDB
docs.text:
Last update: 20261020-1

In this part of O2 tutorial, you will learn the technique for accessing a histogram (or some other ROOT object) at run-time in your analysis task in O2Physics from an external ROOT file, and saving that histogram in the output file of your analysis. Typically, this way you access a histogram with efficiency corrections from an external ROOT file, use information from it during analysis, and then save that histogram in the output file of your analysis. This last part is not a trivial duplication of histograms — it is important that you can easily trace back which efficiency corrections you have used in a given analysis, and that is easiest to achieve without additional bookkeeping if you save that histogram in the output of that analysis.

To master the technique, follow these steps below...

docs.title: 1. Adding new data member in the analysis task.
docs.text: Add among data members of your analysis task in O2Physics a new TH1F histogram, named histWeights (of course, you can generalize and rename later, we now focus only on technicalities).

docs.title: 2. The structure of ROOT file with efficiency corrections.
docs.text:
Make locally a ROOT file, named "weights.root", which has the following internal structure (you can start developing and maintaining a dedicated ROOT macro/executable for this sake, to automate the whole procedure, as some aspects of this internal structure are mandatory):

TList "ccdb_object"
  TList "000123456"
     histWithEfficiencyCorrections_1
     histWithEfficiencyCorrections_2 
     ... more histograms in TList named "000123456" ...
  TList "000654321"
     histWithEfficiencyCorrections_1 
     histWithEfficiencyCorrections_2 
     ... more histograms in TList named "000654321" ...
  ... more nested TLists within TList "ccdb_object" ...

In the above example internal structure of ROOT file "weighs.root":

  • TList "ccdb_object" is the top-level list which contains all other objects in this ROOT file "weights.root" — it has to be named exactly "ccdb_object";
  • TList "000123456" is the example nested TList, which will contain all histograms with efficiency corrections for the particular run number "000123456" (the name of this TList is custom);
  • "histWithEfficiencyCorrections_1" is the first example histogram, with some specific efficiency corrections pertaining to run number "000123456" (e.g. phi-weights, the name of this histogram is custom);
  • "histWithEfficiencyCorrections_2" is the second example histogram, with some other efficiency corrections pertaining to run number "000123456" (e.g. pt-weights, the name of this histogram is custom).
  • ... and so on!

It doesn't matter for the time being which content you will have in the above example histograms "histWithEfficiencyCorrections_*" , what matters is that now you develop the code in your O2Physics analysis task, which will access, use in the analysis at run-time, and copy that histogram from an external ROOT file, into your data member histWeights , and then save it automatically in the output file "AnalysisResults.root" of your analysis, alongside of other booked objects in the analysis task.

docs.title: 3. New configurable.
docs.text:
Add a new configurable to your analysis code using the following code snippet:

Configurable<std::string> cfFileWithWeights{"cfFileWithWeights", "/home/abilandz/DatasetsO2/weights.root", "path to external ROOT file which holds all particle weights"};
For bookkeeping sake, set the title of your data member histogram histWeights to the string stored in your configurable, namely "cfFileWithWeights".

Then, in a JSON configuration file, you would need to have the corresponding new field when you are configuring your analysis task:

 "cfFileWithWeights": "/home/abilandz/DatasetsO2/weights.root",

An external ROOT file "weights.root" can be in three different locations, and after this tutorial, you will master access to that external file for all three cases. An external ROOT file holding efficiency corrections can be:

  1. on your local computer — just use an absolute or relative path to it in the above JSON field

  2. in your home directory in CCDB ("Calibration and Conditions Database"). This is the default, and therefore most important, way to store efficiency corrections. To inspect the content of home directory in CCDB, one can open the following URL address in the browser

    https://alice-ccdb.cern.ch/browse/Users/a/abilandz/

    Just replace in the URL address above "a/abilandz/" with your credentials, and in that browser, a valid certificate needs to be installed. For this case, prepend a file path in the above JSON field with a string "/alice-ccdb.cern.ch/"

  3. in your home directory in AliEn. This works, but it is not allowed to use this approach later in a large-scale data analysis in Hyperloop. Therefore, use this only in a local analysis for testing purposes. For this case, prepend a file path in the above JSON field with a string "/alice/cern.ch/"

The main point behind the above convention in the JSON config of specifying the path of an external file is that now in the analysis code it will be automatically determined from that path whether that external file is on a local compute, in CCDB, or in AliEn. Correspondingly, different code needs to be used to access that file, and that is provided with the function *_TH1F GetHistogramWithWeights(...)_**, which is introduced next.

docs.title: 4. function TH1F* GetHistogramWithWeights(...)
docs.text:
To fetch automatically in your analysis task in O2Physics a histogram with efficiency corrections from an external ROOT file, for any of the three cases of interest mentioned above (local, CCDB, and AliEn), consider incorporating the function _TH1F GetHistogramWithWeights(...)_* below into your analysis task. The latest version of the code can be obtained directly from O2Tutorial repository, by following this direct link. The function is implemented semi-schematically, but it's trivial to finalize yourself all the remaining details:

File: src/cpp/GetHistogramWithWeights.cpp
TH1F* GetHistogramWithWeights(const char* filePath, const char* runNumber)
{
  // Last update: 20261018 

  // *) Return value:
  TH1F* hist = NULL;
  TList* baseList = NULL; // base top-level list in the TFile, e.g. named "ccdb_object"
  TList* listWithRuns = NULL; // nested list with run-wise TList's holding run-specific weights

  // *) Determine from filePath if the file is on a local machine, or in home dir AliEn, or in CCDB:

  //    Algorithm: a) If filePath begins with "/alice/cern.ch/" then it's in the home dir AliEn;
  //               b) If filePath begins with "/alice-ccdb.cern.ch/" then it's in CCDB. Therefore, files in AliEn and CCDB must be specified with abs path;
  //               c) For local files both absolute and relative paths are just fine.

  bool bFileIsInAliEn = false;
  bool bFileIsInCCDB = false;


  // ... implement your own code here for the above Algorithm, 
  //     to determine from the content of filePath where the external file is, 
  //     and reset the above flags bFileIsInAliEn and bFileIsInCCDB correspondingly ...


  if (bFileIsInAliEn) {

​    // File you want to access is in your home directory in AliEn.
    // In this branch, there is a special code to support file access in that case.

​    TGrid* alien = TGrid::Connect("alien", gSystem->Getenv("USER"), "", ""); 
    // For this to work, do not forget to add #include <TGrid.h> to the preamble of your analysis task

​    if (!alien) {
​     LOGF(fatal, "\033[1;31m%s at line %d\033[0m", __FUNCTION__, __LINE__);
​    }
​    TFile* weightsFile = TFile::Open(Form("alien://%s", filePath), "READ"); // yes, ROOT can open a file transparently, even if it's sitting in AliEn, with this specific syntax
​    if (!weightsFile) {
​     LOGF(fatal, "\033[1;31m%s at line %d\033[0m", __FUNCTION__, __LINE__);
​    }
​    weightsFile->GetObject("ccdb_object", baseList);
​    if (!baseList) {
​     // weightsFile->ls();
​     LOGF(fatal, "\033[1;31m%s at line %d\033[0m", __FUNCTION__, __LINE__);
​    }

​    // Finally, from the top-level TList "ccdb_object", get the desired nested TList.
    // The technical problem here is that it can be nested at any level,
​    // to overcome that there is a helper utility function TObject* GetObjectFromList(...),
    // whose implementation if discussed and provided separately.
​    listWithRuns = reinterpret_cast<TList*>(GetObjectFromList(baseList, runNumber));
​    if (!listWithRuns) {
​     TString runNumberWithLeadingZeroes = "000";
​     runNumberWithLeadingZeroes += runNumber; // another try, with "000" prepended to run number
​     listWithRuns = reinterpret_cast<TList*>(GetObjectFromList(baseList, runNumberWithLeadingZeroes.Data()));
​     if (!listWithRuns) {
​     LOGF(fatal, "\033[1;31m%s at line %d\033[0m", __FUNCTION__, __LINE__);
​    }
   }

   // OK, we got the desired run-specific TList with efficiency corrections for AliEn case, 
   // after that we can use the common code for all 3 cases (local, AliEn, CCDB),
   // that common code is further below.

   } else if (bFileIsInCCDB) {

​    // File you want to access is in your home directory in CCDB. 
    // In this branch, there is a special code to support file access in that case.

​    // Remember that here I do not access the file; instead, I directly access the object in that file.
​    // My home dir in CCDB: https://alice-ccdb.cern.ch/browse/Users/a/abilandz/ => adapt for your case
​    ccdb->setURL("http://alice-ccdb.cern.ch"); // to be able to use the "ccdb" object in your analysis task, see further down in this tutorial an explanation
​    baseList = reinterpret_cast<TList*>(ccdb->get<TList>(TString(filePath).ReplaceAll("/alice-ccdb.cern.ch/", "").Data())); 
​    if (!baseList) {
​     LOGF(fatal, "\033[1;31m%s at line %d\033[0m", __FUNCTION__, __LINE__);
​    }

​    listWithRuns = reinterpret_cast<TList*>(GetObjectFromList(baseList, runNumber));
​    if (!listWithRuns) {
​    TString runNumberWithLeadingZeroes = "000";
​    runNumberWithLeadingZeroes += runNumber; // another try, with "000" prepended to run number
​    listWithRuns = reinterpret_cast<TList*>(GetObjectFromList(baseList, runNumberWithLeadingZeroes.Data()));
​    if (!listWithRuns) {
​     LOGF(fatal, "\033[1;31m%s at line %d\033[0m", __FUNCTION__, __LINE__);
​    }
   }

   // OK, we got the desired run-specific TList with efficiency corrections for CCDB, 
   // after that we can use the common code for all 3 cases (local, AliEn, CCDB),
   // that common code is further below.

   } else {

​    // File you want to access is on your local computer. 
    // In this branch, there is a special code to support file access in that case.

​    // Check if the external ROOT file exists at the specified path:
​    if (gSystem->AccessPathName(filePath, kFileExists)) {
​     LOGF(info, "\033[1;33m if(gSystem->AccessPathName(filePath,kFileExists)), filePath = %s \033[0m", filePath);
​     LOGF(fatal, "\033[1;31m%s at line %d\033[0m", __FUNCTION__, __LINE__);
​    }

​    TFile* weightsFile = TFile::Open(filePath, "READ");
​    if (!weightsFile) {
​     LOGF(fatal, "\033[1;31m%s at line %d\033[0m", __FUNCTION__, __LINE__);
​    }

​    weightsFile->GetObject("ccdb_object", baseList);

    if (!baseList) {
    // weightsFile->ls();
    LOGF(fatal, "\033[1;31m%s at line %d\033[0m", __FUNCTION__, __LINE__);
   }

   listWithRuns = reinterpret_cast<TList*>(GetObjectFromList(baseList, runNumber));
   if (!listWithRuns) {
    TString runNumberWithLeadingZeroes = "000";
    runNumberWithLeadingZeroes += runNumber; // another try, with "000" prepended to run number
    listWithRuns = reinterpret_cast<TList*>(GetObjectFromList(baseList, runNumberWithLeadingZeroes.Data()));
    if (!listWithRuns) {
     // baseList->ls();
     LOGF(fatal, "\033[1;31m%s at line %d : this crash can happen if in the output file there is no list with weights for the current run number = %s\033[0m", __FUNCTION__, __LINE__, tc.fRunNumber.Data());
    }
   }

   // OK, we got the desired run-specific TList with efficiency corrections for local case, 
   // after that we can use the common code for all 3 cases (local, AliEn, CCDB),
   // that common code is further below.

  } // end of else

  // The common code for all three cases, where from "listWithRuns" you fetch the desired histogram with efficiency corrections:
  // listWithRuns->ls();


  // ... implement your own code to get pointer to "hist" object from TList *listWithRuns" 
  //     (it was declared at the beginning of this function "TH1F* hist = NULL;"   
  //     Once you have a valid pointer to "hist", add the technical lines below.


  hist->SetDirectory(0); // remove ownerhip from an external file
  TH1F* histClone = reinterpret_cast<TH1F*>(hist->Clone()); // yes, I have to clone here

  delete baseList; // release back the memory

  return histClone;

} // end of TH1F* GetHistogramWithWeights(...)

docs.title: 5. Usage of the "ccdb" object in analysis task.
docs.text:
To be able to use the "ccdb" object in your analysis task, add the following line in the preamble among other include directives:

#include <CCDB/BasicCCDBManager.h>
Then afterward in the code, add this line just after you have started the struct definition of your analysis task: 
Service<ccdb::BasicCCDBManager> ccdb;

After these additions., you call the above function _TH1F GetHistogramWithWeights(...)_* in your analysis code to initialize the data member histWeights (introduced in 1. above) as follows:

histWeights = GetHistogramWithWeights(cfFileWithWeights, "some-run-number");

After that, you can use at runtime information from histWeights which was initialized with information from an external ROOT file. At the end of the analysis, histWeights will be automaticaly saved in the output of your analysis alongside other data members.

docs.title: 6. function TObject* GetObjectFromList(...)
docs.text:
Finally, the implementation of the utility function _TObject GetObjectFromList(...)_* is below. The latest version of the code can be obtained directly from O2Tutorial repository, by following this direct link GetObjectFromList.cpp. Incorporate this function's implementation to your analysis task as well:

File src/cpp/GetObjectFromList.cpp
TObject* GetObjectFromList(TList* list, const char* objectName)
{
 // Last update: 20261018 

 // Get TObject pointer from TList, even if it's in some nested TList. 
 // Foreseen to be used to fetch histograms or profiles from files directly. 

 // Some ideas taken from TCollection::ls()

 // If you have added histograms directly to files (without TList's), then you can fetch them directly with
 // file->Get("hist-name").

 // Example usage: TH1D *hist = (TH1D*) GetObjectFromList("some-valid-TList-pointer","some-object-name");

 // Insanity checks:
 if (!list) {
  LOGF(fatal, "\033[1;31m%s at line %d\033[0m", __FUNCTION__, __LINE__);
 }
 if (!objectName) {
  LOGF(fatal, "\033[1;31m%s at line %d\033[0m", __FUNCTION__, __LINE__);
 }
 if (0 == list->GetEntries()) {
  return NULL;
 }

 // The object is in the current base list:
 TObject* objectFinal = list->FindObject(objectName); // the final object I am after
 if (objectFinal ) { return objectFinal; }

 // Otherwise, search for the object recursively in the nested lists:
 TObject* objectIter; // iterator object in the loop below
 TIter next(list);
 while ((objectIter = next())) // double round braces are to silence the warnings
 {
  if (TString(objectIter->ClassName()).EqualTo("TList")) {
   objectFinal = GetObjectFromList(reinterpret_cast<TList*>(objectIter), objectName);
   if (objectFinal)
    return objectFinal;
  }
 } // while(objectIter = next())

 return NULL;

} // TObject* GetObjectFromList(...)

docs.title: 7. Shell utility function UploadFileToCCDB
docs.text:
To upload a file in CCDB, the Bash shell utility function UploadFileToCCDB can be used. That function is implemented, alongside other O2 utility functions in O2Tutorial repository, and the latest version of the code can be obtained directly by following this direct link O2.sh.

To use it, follow these steps:

a) Initialize locally the O2 environment using shell function MenuO2

b) Source the implementation of all functions: 

$ source O2.sh # adapt the path to this file

c) Dump the config file of function UploadFileToCCDB in the current working directory. To execute this step, you must have a valid certificate in place to access ALICE Grid (see this section TBI 20261019 finalize this part): 

$ UploadFileToCCDB -h

d) The config file "UploadFileToCCDB.config" have the following variables and example content: File src/scripts/UploadFileToCCDB.config

# Path to the file which will be uploaded:
local File="../root/labels.root"

# Relative path to the top-level directory in CCDB where 
# file will be uploaded (relative to CCDB host below):
local RelativePath="Users/a/abilandz/test-tmp"

# CCDB host:
local Host_CCDB="alice-ccdb.cern.ch"

# Corresponding AliEn dir:
local AliEnDir_CCDB="/alice/data/CCDB/Users/a/abilandz"

# Key:
local Key="ccdb_object"

# Start timestamp of validity (set to -1 or to 0 for valid as of now):
local StartTimeStamp="-1"

# End timestamp of validity in days from start timestamp
# (set e.g. 7 for 7 days):
local EndTimeStamp="7"
It is mandatory to replace "a/abilandz" with your user credentials in AliEn (both in variables "RelativePath" and in "AliEnDir_CCDB"), and adapt a path to the local file you want to upload (in variable "File").

e) After the config file "UploadFileToCCDB.config" is edited, simply execute 

$ UploadFileToCCDB UploadFileToCCDB.config

docs.title: 8. CCDB challenge
docs.text:
a) Prepare example histogram with efficiency corrections, and save it to the file "weights.root" (see Section 2. above).

b) Copy over that file "weights.root" into some local dir, then to AliEn, and finally upload it to CCDB.

c) Ideally, for all three cases, and given the above implementation, you should be able to access histogram with efficiency corrections from that file just by modifying the path in the JSON configurable "cfFileWithWeights", initialize your data member histogram histWeights with its content, and save it in the output of your analysis.

d) The very same technique will work later in the online analysis using Hyperloop, to fetch efficiency corrections at run-time from an external file — only in that case it's mandatory to use CCDB access.

docs.title: How to commit the local code to central O2 repository?
docs.text:
Last update: 20261022-1

Here are the steps you need to follow to commit your code from the local O2Physics repository to the centrall O2Physics repository at https://github.com/AliceO2Group/O2Physics.

The main point is that once your code is in the central O2Physics repository, and then shortly afterward in one of the daily release tags, your code can be used to analyze large datasets online in Hyperloop.

Disclaimer #1: Some of the steps below are needed only the very first time you commit your code.

Disclaimer #2: In addition, some steps below can be optimized and further improved using Git built-in functionalities, but I give you now the version which works, see later yourself if you want to optimize it further yourself.

docs.title: 1. Setting up the GitHub account.
docs.text:
First, in case you already do not have it, you need to create an account on GitHub (ideally, by using the same username as you have at CERN, but that is not mandatory).

After that, login in your GitHub account and authorize "ALICE Continuous Integration" to read your username so that it can be mapped to your CERN account (for more details, see the first two sections in https://alisw.github.io/git-tutorial/.

On your computer where you are developing the code in the O2Physics repository and where you can run 'git', adapt your credentials and then execute:

git config --global user.name "<Firstname> <Lastname>" 
git config --global user.email <your-CERN-email-address> 
git config --global user.github <your-GitHub-username>

docs.title: 2. Forking.
docs.text:
In this step, you will learn how to clone the central O2Physics repository on GitHub into your own account on GitHub, a process called 'forking'.

a) Go to the central O2Physics repository on GitHub by following this link https://github.com/AliceO2Group/O2Physics ;

b) Click on the 'Fork' in the top-half-right corner (you can click only if you are already logged in GitHub, if not just click on the top on 'Sign in');

c) If forking went OK, now you shall be automatically redirected to something like https://github.com/abilandz/O2Physics (adapt the username for your own account, same comments applies wherever below you see 'abilandz'). This is your personal 'fork' for O2Physics repository, of central O2Physics repository at https://github.com/AliceO2Group/O2Physics.

d) At the time you 'forked' the central repository, your own 'fork' is the 'master' version of https://github.com/AliceO2Group/O2Physics at the time you did the fork. Few remarks:

  • New changes in central 'master' are NOT automatically propagated into your own 'fork' — this is summarized in your 'fork' with something like "This branch is ... ahead and ... behind AliceO2Group/O2Physics:master"
  • The point of having 'fork' is the following: You can propagate changes from your local O2Physics repository directly into the online O2Physics repository, but only in your own 'fork' (certainly NOT in the central O2Physics repository).
  • Only when you want to propagate those changes to the central repository https://github.com/AliceO2Group/O2Physics, a lot of automated checks will be performed, and a person in charge needs to review and approve them
  • In the browser, see if you want to bookmark your own 'fork', as you will be visiting this page frequently.
  • If you have screwed-up your 'fork', or if your 'fork' is lagging too much behind the development in https://github.com/AliceO2Group/O2Physics , no worries, you can trivally always delete your 'fork', and make a new 'fork' again (or you can use built-in functionalities in Git to synchronize, investigate this further by yourself if interested — at least in the beginning, keep it simple and just delete your fork and fork it again). To delete a 'fork', just go to your 'fork' online, then click on 'Settings' (last item in the close-to-top horizontal menu), then scroll down to the 'Danger Zone' and opt for 'Delete this repository'. Then, simply go to Step 2a) again.

To synchronize local 'master' version of O2Physics with the 'forked' master of O2Physics online in GitHub, the typical/standard workflow during code development is the following:

  • Make some changes in your analysis task in the local 'master' => propagate those changes to 'forked master' online => propagate online changes from 'forked master' to the 'central master' by creating a pull request (needs several reviews and official approval)

  • How to establish the link between 'forked master' in GitHub, with the local 'master' (here I assume that you have checked out already on your desktop 'master' of O2Physics with the standard scripts I gave you — you do NOT need to recompile this 'master' version from scratch, you can use something like this in the shell function InstallationO2:

    InstallationO2_TopLevelBuildDir=someDirectory; InstallationO2_Compile=false; InstallationO2 master

  • Go to the local git repository of your O2Physics 'master' (remember - you do NOT need to compile it from scratch, just check it out locally):

    # use the same path as above:
cd someDirectory

# 'abilandz' here is my GitHub account name, replace with yours:
git remote add abilandz git@github.com:abilandz/O2Physics 

# In order to cross-check if your local 'master' is now in sync. 
# with 'forked master' in GitHub, type:
git remote -v

    The printout shall be like below (first two lines are your 'fork', and the last two lines are the central repository: 

    # if you have only the last two lines, the previous step has failed):
abilandz git@github.com:abilandz/O2Physics (fetch)
abilandz git@github.com:abilandz/O2Physics (push)
upstream https://github.com/AliceO2Group/O2Physics (fetch)
upstream https://github.com/AliceO2Group/O2Physics (push)

docs.title: 3. Setting up a passwordless login for GitHub using SSH.
docs.text:
You need to perform this step if you do not want to type your password again and again when connecting to GitHub from your terminal => basically, you need to follow these online instructions:

  • https://help.github.com/articles/checking-for-existing-ssh-keys/
  • https://help.github.com/articles/generating-a-new-ssh-key-and-adding-it-to-the-ssh-agent/
  • https://help.github.com/articles/adding-a-new-ssh-key-to-your-github-account/

docs.title: 4. Propagating changes from 'local master' into 'forked master' on GitHub.
docs.text:
If necessary, you can remind yourself about Git by having a look at the first two sections of https://nat3054-ws2627.onrender.com/git.html.

Do some change in your 'local master' where you are regularly developing your code. By default, modify locally ONLY your code, do NOT touch the code of other people!! After you have reviewed and validated your code in your working repository locally, copy only the modified classes into a temporary git repository (named "someDirectory" in step 2b/ above - remember, this one you do NOT compile, you just use it to propagate local changes to your online 'fork'):

Simply do in the terminal:

cd someDirectory/O2Physics # this is the top O2Physics directory
git status # execute this command to get a summary of all classes which have been changed
git add someCode.cxx # indicate here which code you have modified (in the git vocabulary, you are staging your changes)
git add someOtherCode.cxx # indicate here which code you have modified (in the git vocabulary, you are staging your changes)
git commit -m "some nice commit message" # commit all that you have staged at the previous step. 
git push abilandz # finally, move your changes from 'local master' to 'forked master' on Grid (use your username here)

After this point, changes are on your own 'fork' on GitHub (check now the updated status of your fork on GitHub!), and they are not yet upstream in the central O2Physics repository on GitHub. This means they will not be included in the daily tag, unless you do not perform the next, and the final, step.

When for the very first time you are adding a new class to the central O2 repository, you also need to add to your commit the modified specific "CMakeLists.txt file", remember from one of the previous tutorials the lines below...

  • copy class student-o2physics.cxx into subdir ~/scratch/aliceO2-1/O2Physics/PWGCF/MultiparticleCorrelations/Tasks

  • in that subdir, there is a file "CMakeLists.txt" . Append the following lines end the end of that file:

o2physics_add_dpl_workflow(student-o2physics
                    SOURCES student-o2physics.cxx
                    PUBLIC_LINK_LIBRARIES O2::Framework O2Physics::AnalysisCore O2Physics::PWGCFCore
                    COMPONENT_NAME Analysis)

By this point, think of a new name for your analysis task, i.e. you can rename "student-o2physics.cxx" into any other name you would prefer, and propagate that change in all other files. In case you have renamed your analysis task "student-o2physics.cxx" into some other file name, use that new name above in "CMakeLists.txt" as well.

docs.title: 5. Propagating changes from 'forked master' on GitHub into 'central master' on GitHub (a.k.a. 'New Pull Request')
docs.text:
• Simply go to your fork of O2Physics on GitHub, click 'Contribute', and then select 'Open Pull Request', and follow the tide.

  • After all automated checks in the central repository related to your pull request are successful, and after somebody in charge (the official reviewer) approves your pull request (PR), your code is in the 'master' of the central O2 repository, and it will be included automatically in the next release tag. This procedure can take easily more than 1 day, so you need to be patient. If any of the automated checks failed, you have to fix your code locally immediately, make a new commit, and that commit will be automatically included in the same pull request.

  • The final email you shall receive shall contain the message like this: Merged #13241 into master. This means that your change is now propagated in the 'central master' of O2Physics on GitHub.

  • If your change was propagated before 16:00, it will be included in the daily analysis tag, and typically by 20:00 of the same day, it will be deployed all over the Grid (but delays can happen). After this point, you can also use your latest changes on Hyperloop!

Try to go by yourself ONLY through steps 1-4. Send me the link to your online 'fork' (give me also access permission, if necessary), which has a commit with all the changes you want to propagate to the central repository via pull request, but please DO NOT execute the pull request yet. I will review your changes and provide feedback.

The very last step 5/ we will do together (only the first time).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Last update: 20261008-1

1/ We ported two functions to your account, InstallationO2 and MenuO2, and started from scratch your first local O2 compilation on /scratch disk area. Once the compilation finishes, please try to open a new terminal on 'nidoqueen', or a new window in the existing screen session (in both cases you get a new shell instance with a clean environment!), and use the MenuO2 function to enable the O2 environment in that new and clean shell. If MenuO2 succeeded, remember that you still have to type 

$ bash

in the terminal, to finalize environment initialization.

2/ Remember to keep in sync all default values for relevant variables (e.g. top-level directory for O2 compilation) in both InstallationO2 and MenuO2.

3/ There is another presentation from the latest O2 tutorial in November 2025: https://indico.cern.ch/event/1574136/timetable/ you can consult now (in case you do not have access, I have uploaded this 2nd presentation by David at the same public link ). Please have a look at the first 10 slides, and try to execute the tutorial executable (which shall be ready to use in your environment if compilation went through, and O2 environment is correctly initialized e.g. with MenuO2 function) to: a) process one example AOD2.root file. It's explained on the slides from David how to download it from his Dropbox - if his link expired, please try to process this local file: /scratch3/abilandz/O2/Datasets/Run_3/2023/LHC23zzh/544122/apass3/0440/o2_ctf_run00544122_orbit0160006240_tf0000749850_epn059/003/AO2D.root b) as an output of this processing, try to produce a ROOT file automatically, holding a histogram with example eta distribution. Please send me that eta distribution by email!

docs.title: O2 coding style and rules, O2linter, etc.
docs.text:
Last update: 20261021-1

In this part of the O2 tutorial, O2 coding style and rules are covered, and usage of related software (e.g. O2linter) is introduced. From the very beginning, you need to conform to the official O2 coding style and rules, otherwise, you won't be able to contribute the code to the central O2 repository.

docs.title: 1. Common code formatting.
docs.text:
For common code formatting, use locally:

$ clang-format -i someFile

If you do not already have it installed, the command clang-format is available after you initialize the O2 environment. The flag -i will modify your file in-place (i.e. it will reformat the file and then overwrite the original file) — this is potentially dangerous, therefore see if you want to develop a shell script, which will first make a backup of "someFile", before in that script you call clang-format for that file.

docs.title: 2. Running O2linter locally.
docs.text:
When you eventually create a pull request for your code to be included into the official O2 repository https://github.com/AliceO2Group/O2Physics, so that you can use your code in the Hyperloop in online analysis, it will go first through ~10 automated checks, before your pull request will be approved. One automated test that will be added in the near future as mandatory is O2linter (still under development!), you can find a summary of its current status in Vít Kučera slides (i uploaded them in the following same public online directory). Do NOT get lost in the details, the most important slides are 11, 12, 18, and particularly 24.

To run O2linter locally, simply use:

# adapt the path below to your working git repository
# in which you compile and run the code:
$ cd ~/scratch/aliceO2-12/O2Physics
$ python3 Scripts/o2_linter.py PWGCF/MultiparticleCorrelations/Tasks/<your-task>

From the very beginning, try to implement locally all O2linter suggestions, etc.

docs.title: 3. O2 coding guidelines.
docs.text: Check also https://github.com/AliceO2Group/CodingGuidelines and references therein.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Last update: 20261008-1

This is introductory material for the O2 analysis framework: * Official documentation for the ALICE O2 Analysis Framework is maintained at this link: https://aliceo2group.github.io/analysis-framework/ * the low-level O2 tables to which you can subscribe directly in the analysis code are at this link; * helper-task tables that you have to include in the workflow explicitly are at this link, etc.

  • Latest O2 tutorial, November 2025: https://indico.cern.ch/event/1574136/timetable/ (in case you do not have access, I have uploaded the intro presentation by David, which is the most important material in any case, at this public link ).

Please play a bit, look around, and see what you think. But please be selective, because you will need 10% of all these functionalities in practice.
